claims.text: Structural and chemical stability of initially solid-solution nanoparticles containing at least five metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios is governed by entropy stabilization.
Entropy stabilization suppresses phase segregation across 473–1923 K.
Entropy stabilization suppresses structural transformations across 473–1923 K.
The proposed starting materials are nanoparticles containing five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios and crystallized as a solid solution.
The nanoparticles will be subjected to temperatures from 473 K to 1923 K under inert or reactive atmospheres.
No external mechanical stress will be applied during thermal exposure.
The solid-solution phase has high configurational entropy.
High configurational entropy reduces the thermodynamic driving force for phase segregation.
High configurational entropy reduces the thermodynamic driving force for structural transformations.
The nanoparticles will retain their solid-solution structure throughout exposure from 473 K to 1923 K.
The nanoparticles will exhibit minimal phase segregation throughout exposure from 473 K to 1923 K.
The nanoparticles will exhibit minimal structural transformation throughout exposure from 473 K to 1923 K.
The initial baseline has no observable phase segregation or structural transformation.
The prediction is expected to hold only when the temperature remains below the alloy melting point.
The prediction is expected to hold only in the absence of extreme surface-diffusion effects.
Specific metal combinations, melting points, and diffusion coefficients may influence nanoparticle stability.
Significant phase segregation or structural transformation after inert-atmosphere heating would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis and prediction broadly claim stability through 1923 K, while the boundary limits the claim to temperatures below the unspecified melting point and without extreme surface diffusion. Thus, the full stated range is not guaranteed for alloys whose melting point or diffusion limit lies below 1923 K.
